answer: Use the sc-rx command, which shows the Receiving Secure Channel attributes: show sc-rx-<name>/<index> [sci-rx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]. The 'state' attribute is what tells you whether the channel is in use; it is the state returned by the MKA stack and takes the values in-use (Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use) or not-in-use (no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use). The AID combines name, a string of length 0..64, with index, the Receiving Secure Channel Index, a uint8. sci-rx is the Receiving Secure Channel Identifier, a 16-character hex-string. sc-rx is show-only and is available in both Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

sc-tx reports the Transmitting Secure Channel attributes and is show-only; there is no add, set or delete form. The syntax is show sc-tx-<name>/<index> [sci-tx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]. name is a string of length 0..64 and index is the Transmitting Secure Channel Index, a uint8. sci-tx is the Transmitting Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16. state is the state of the secure channel returned by the MKA stack, either in-use (Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use) or not-in-use (no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use). Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

A secure-application is an application that uses an X509v3 certificate as its digital identity. The certificate it presents is set with active-certificate-id, a string of length 0..128 holding the list of assigned certificates: set secure-application-<id> active-certificate-id <value>. For example set secure-application-WebGUI active-certificate-id client, or a comma-separated list such as set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY. The in-use attribute (a leafref to ../active-certificate-id) shows which one is actually active. To require a certificate from clients, set verify-client-cert, which enables TLS Mutual Authentication: disabled means no client certificate is requested (the default), required means the client certificate is required and validated and must be used for TLS Mutual Authentication. Changes to verify-client-cert take effect only for new TLS connections and have no impact on existing ones. Other show-only attributes are type (server or client) and status (enabled or disabled); show secure-applications lists them all.

That is controlled by re-key-fail-policy on the secure-entity, which indicates the NE's policy and consequent action when re-keying the IKE security association is unsuccessful. Values are kill-traffic and continue-traffic, and the default is continue-traffic, so by default traffic is not dropped. If you set kill-traffic, the traffic-kill-offset attribute gives the amount of time the system waits before killing all encrypted data security associations tied to that IKE SA; its range is 0..86400 seconds and it defaults to 0. Both are settable on add and set, for example: add secure-entity-NE202-1-4-L1-1 supporting-facility optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1 remote-secure-entity '1-4-L1-1' re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic traffic-kill-offset 300. The related re-key-frequency for the IKE SA with the far-end IKE peer ranges 3600..86400 seconds, default 28800.

No. secure-entity-sa-proposal is show-only: show secure-entity-sa-proposal-<name>/<number> [encryption-algorithm] [encryption-key-length] [integrity-algorithm] [dh-group]. Every algorithm attribute has exactly one permitted value, which is also its default: encryption-algorithm is aes-gcm-16; encryption-key-length is key-length-256; integrity-algorithm is none; and dh-group, the Diffie-Hellman group advertised to the far-end secure entity peer, is ecp-521. The proposal number likewise has the single value 1, default 1. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. So the layer 1 wavelength encryption suite is fixed and you can only display it, not change it.

Through the security-policy-database object, whose key is the pair <ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name>: ikev2-local-instance is the name (ID) of the local IKE protocol daemon instance and ikev2-peer is a reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA). The tie to the encrypted entity is the associated-secure-entity attribute, the list of all SPD entries associated with that far-end peer for which IKE negotiates security associations (keys). Syntax: add security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name> [associated-secure-entity <value>], with matching set, show and delete forms. Example on 1830 GX G40: add security-policy-database-ikev2-local-instance-1-6/ikev2-NE202-1-4 associated-secure-entity secure-entity-1-6-L1-1. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. Use the cdp command to manage manually configured CRL Distribution Points; each CDP supports download and auto-refreshing of a specified CRL. Syntax: add cdp-<name> url <value> [enabled <value>] [refresh-interval <value>], plus set, delete, show cdp-<name> and show cdps. url is the HTTP URL of the CRL in the form 'http://<host>[:<port>]/<path to crl file>', for example http://crl.example.org/pki/myCA.crl. enabled (true, false, default false) turns on automatic download and periodic refresh; enabling immediately triggers a CRL auto-download, and when disabled no refresh or updates are performed although existing CRLs are unaffected. refresh-interval either takes the special enum value use-next-update, meaning the next refresh time comes from the current CRL's next-update field, or a string in the form '[xw] [xd] [xh] [xm] [xs]' such as 2w, '5d 12h' or '1h 7m 30s'. show also returns next-update-time, last-update-time and last-update-result. Requires System Administrator privilege.

Use cert-gen, an Operational mode command: cert-gen [-f] [certificate-name=]<value> [[days=]<value>] [[org-name=]<value>] [[common-name=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [SAN=]<value>] [auto-install <true|false>]. Validity is set by days, the number of days the certificate is valid for, which defaults to 365. certificate-name is a string of length 1..128, org-name a string of 1..64, common-name the IP or host name identifying the server (1..64), and subject the full certificate subject name (1..1024). When generating a self-signed certificate you must specify either subject or common-name. auto-install (true/false, default true) auto-assigns the certificate to any secure-application that has no active certificate. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. Example: cert-gen -f certificate-name=self-signed-cert1 days=10 org-name=testorg common-name=testcert auto-install=true.

Through cert-to-name, which defines a prioritized set of rules mapping an X.509 client certificate to a specific user identity. Each rule either extracts a username from a certificate field or maps it directly, or matches on a specific issuer in the certificate's trust chain. Syntax: add cert-to-name-<id> map-type <value> field <value> mapped-user-name <value> criteria <value> [priority <value>] [issuer <value>] [enabled <value>] [label <value>], with set, delete and show. map-type is extract or map. field applies only when map-type is extract and selects the certificate attribute used to determine the identity: common-name, san-any, san-dns-name, san-ip-address, san-rfc822-name, san-upn or san-uri. mapped-user-name is required only when map-type is map and gives the local or remote user identity. criteria defines the attributes and conditions required for the rule to be invoked. priority ranges 1 to 255. issuer takes the value any and adds a restriction filtering certificates from a specific issuer. enabled defaults to True. Example: add cert-to-name-rule_name map-type extract field san-dns-name.

Use the certificate command in Operational mode. To remove one: clear [-f] certificate [type=]<value> [id=]<value>. type is trusted, local or peer; id is the certificate ID, a string of length 0..128, and it must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type (press <tab> to list the certificate-ids that can be cleared). -f forces the command without confirmation, otherwise you get an 'Are you sure? [y/n]' prompt. Examples: clear certificate local certX, clear certificate type=trusted id=certY, clear certificate trusted id=root. type also accepts bulk purge options: purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused. To list what is installed, use show certificates, which displays all managed local/trusted/peer X509v3 certificates imported by the download mechanism in PKCS#12 or PKCS#7 secure bundles; show certificate-revocation shows certificate revocations.

Use the clear form of the crl command with a clear-target that selects a class of CRLs: clear [-f] crl [[clear-target=]<value>] [crl-name=]<value>. The targets are single-crl (remove the CRL named in <crl-name>; this is the default and <crl-name> is then mandatory and must match a currently installed CRL), purge-invalid-crls (purge all invalid CRLs), purge-cached-crls (purge all CRLs that were automatically cached from a configured CDP or a certificate CDP extension), and purge-all-crls (purge all CRLs). To drop only stale entries, use purge-invalid-crls, for example: clear crl purge-invalid-crls. To remove one by name: clear crl single-crl myCA-1. Use <tab> to obtain the list of CRL names that can be cleared. Check status first with show crls or show crl-<name>, where status is valid, expired or future and type is cached or manually. The clear form runs in Operational mode; show also works in Candidate Configuration mode.

csr-gen creates a local-certificate in the 'pending-import' state and outputs a CSR in PKCS#10 PEM format. That CSR is then given to an external Certificate Authority to produce a full certificate, which is downloaded back into the system to produce a complete local-certificate. Until that import happens the local-certificate stays in pending-import, which is also reported as the status attribute of local-certificate ('If CSR pending - pending-import'). Syntax: csr-gen [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [subject=]<value>] [[SAN=]<value>] and so on. key-algorithm defaults to eccp256 (choices rsa2048, rsa3072, rsa4096, eccp128, eccp256, eccp384, eccp521); metadata-template defaults to generic; key-usage defaults to digitalSignature,keyAgreement and extended-key-usage to serverAuth,clientAuth. The subject must include the CN RDN. Operational mode only. Example: csr-gen myCertificate subject='/CN=Nokia'.

Use display-cert with the display-type parameter: display-cert [certificate=]<value> [display-type=]<value>. display-type accepts all-certificate-hierarchy, certificate-details and certificate-hierarchy, and defaults to all-certificate-hierarchy, so the trust chain view is what you get if you do not specify anything. Choose certificate-hierarchy for the chain of that one certificate, all-certificate-hierarchy for the full hierarchy, and certificate-details when you want only the certificate's own fields (version, serial number, signature algorithm, issuer, validity, subject, public key info and X509v3 extensions). certificate is a string naming the certificate to display, for example display-cert trusted-certificate-ca_root; pressing tab after display-cert lists the available names such as local-certificate-server_cert and trusted-certificate-ca_root. The command also displays CSRs and runs in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the est command. Enrollment over Secure Transport enables automated certificate management over HTTPS and replaces the manual CSR process; the device has an EST client that talks to a dedicated EST server. Syntax: est [target-command=]<value> [[est-ca=]<value>] [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [[SAN=]<value>] [[key-usage=]...] [[extended-key-usage=]...] [[http-user=]<value>] [[http-password=]<value>]. target-command is the operation: cacerts, enroll or re-enroll. est-ca identifies the CA set for EST and defaults to 1. key-algorithm choices are eccp256, eccp384, eccp251, rsa2048, rsa3072, rsa4096; signature-hash-algorithm is sha512, sha384 or sha256, default sha256; metadata-template defaults to generic. Use http-user and http-password when no valid mTLS certificate exists. Example: est enroll certificate-name=myNewCertificateA subject='/CN=NewCertA' http-user=<username> http-password=<password>.

Yes, via auto-re-enrollment on est-ca: set est-ca-<name> [explicit-ca-root <value>] [root-fingerprint <value>] [auto-re-enrollment <value>] [label <value>]. auto-re-enrollment specifies how far before expiration re-enrollment is performed for all leaf certificates issued by that EST CA. It takes either a number of days before expiration from 1 to 365, or a percentage of the 'not after date' minus 'not before date' interval rounded up, accepted from 10% to 90% in increments of 10%, or disabled. The default is Disabled, so automatic re-enrollment is off until you set it. If auto re-enrollment fails for any reason the RE-ENROLL-FAIL alarm is raised for the affected certificate and re-enrollment is retried once per day until it succeeds or the certificate becomes invalid, for example by expiring. The CA is pinned with explicit-ca-root, the trusted root certificate for the EST CA, and root-fingerprint, which verifies the identity of the Root CA using a SHA-256 or SHA-512 hash to ensure a secure initial connection. Example: set est-ca-1 auto-re-enrollment 40.

The EST server port is set by server-port on the est-server command and defaults to 443. Yes, you can define more than one server: the key is <name>/<server-name>, so add est-server-<name>/<server-name> server-address <value> [server-port <value>] [priority <value>] [enabled <value>] [path-segment <value>], with matching set, delete and show forms. priority defines the server's precedence, range 1 to 10; if omitted it defaults to the current lowest precedence (the highest existing number) plus one, and if a priority of 10 already exists the value must be configured manually. enabled is True or False and defaults to True. path-segment is an optional label added to the EST base url, a string of length 0..64. server-address is the IP address of the EST server. Example: add est-server-1/my-est-server server-address 10.23.55.123 server-port 8443. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use import-certificate, which imports one or more certificates in PEM format directly into the NE: import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]; import-certificate -h displays help. The certificate types are local-certificate, trusted-certificate and peer-certificate. certificate-name is the name by which the certificate will be known in the system. passphrase applies to trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundles and decodes encrypted input certificates. The -i flag imports any intermediate certificates present in a PEM string bundle; for a single certificate it imports intermediates specified through the AIA extension. Root certificates must be installed individually. If no certificate-name is given, the name is derived from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix, for instance /CN=Nokia yields trusted-certificate-Nokia-1 and trusted-certificate-Nokia-2. Examples: import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=local-cert-1 <string in PEM format> <passphrase>; import-certificate trusted-certificate certificate-name=bundle-1 -i <string in PEM format>. Operational mode.

Show the key first and check its flags: show ISK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [is-key-in-use] [is-key-verified] [being-deleted] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time], or show ISKs for the list. is-key-in-use indicates whether the key is in use in this FRU (true/false, default false), is-key-verified indicates whether the key is verified in this FRU (true/false, default false), and being-deleted is set to true once the system receives an ISK delete command, meaning the system is in the process of deletion and will soon delete this ISK. KRK-name names the Image Root Key that signed this ISK. To remove one: clear [-f] isk [key-name=]<value>, where key-name is a string of length 0..64 and -f forces the command without confirmation. Example: show ISK-1-5-0-ISK_E1, then clear isk key-name=name. show works in both Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode; clear is Operational only.

Use the KRK commands, which show the list of Image Root Keys (KRKs) and KRK information: show KRKs lists them all, and show KRK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] shows one, for example show KRK-1-5-0-KRK_E1. The attributes are CPU, the identifier for member CPUs on cards, starting at 0 (uint8); key-name, the name of the key, a string of length 0..64; key-serial-number; issuer-name, the name of the CSA (Code Signing Appliance), a string of length 0..20; key-length, the key length in bits (uint16); and key-payload, the key payload in hex format, a string of length 0..1100. KRK is show-only, available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The KRK is the root key that signs ISKs, and each ISK reports its signer in its KRK-name attribute.

The key-replacement-package command shows key replacement package (KRP) attributes: show key-replacement-package [KRP-name] [KRP-version] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time] [install-status]. install-status indicates whether this KRP has been installed in the system and takes the values not-installed, installing, installed and failed. signature-hash-scheme is SHA2 256, SHA2 384 or SHA2 512; signature-algorithm is ECDSA, RSA or none; signature-payload is a hex string of length 0..1024; signature-gen-time is a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ. KRK-name is the name of the KRK (Image root key) that signed this ISK, issuer-name is the CSA (Code Signing Appliance) name, a string of length 0..20, and KRP-version is the package version. The command is show-only and runs in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, with the revocation-mode attribute on local-certificate: set local-certificate-<id> [revocation-mode <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]. revocation-mode controls how the revocation status of the certificate is determined and takes auto, force-revoked or force-unrevoked, with auto as the default. Set force-revoked to make the node treat the certificate as revoked regardless of CRL or OCSP results, and force-unrevoked to force the opposite. The same attribute with the same values and the same auto default exists on peer-certificate. Check the result with show local-certificate-<id> revocation-mode status, where status reports pending-import, expired, revoked, untrusted, future or valid. Other settable attributes are alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed) and label (string 0..256). The id is a string of length 1..128. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use ocsp-server: add ocsp-server-<name> url <value> priority <value> [enabled <value>], with set ocsp-server-<name> [priority <value>] [enabled <value>], delete ocsp-server-<name>, show ocsp-server and show ocsp-server-<name> [url] [enabled] [priority] [last-query]. Order is controlled by priority, a uint8 in the range 1..10 used to sort the OCSP responders in order of precedence: lower numbered OCSP responders are consulted before higher numbered ones, so priority 1 is tried first. url is the HTTP URL of the OCSP responder in the form 'http://<host>[:<port>]', where host may be an IPv4/v6 address or DNS name and the port is optional, otherwise the default HTTP port 80 is used; the string is 0..1024 with pattern 'http://([^\s/$.?#][^\s/]*)'. enabled (true, false, default false) controls whether this server is consulted for revocation status. last-query shows the timestamp of the last successful query, or never. Example: add ocsp-server-1 url http://1.2.3.4:8101 priority 3 enabled true.

A peer-certificate is the X509v3 end-entity certificate that represents a trusted 'remote peer' certificate for the L1 encryption secure application. The white-listed attribute is show-only, true or false with default false: if true, the peer-certificate does not have an associated trust-chain and was explicitly white-listed at import time; otherwise it has an associated trust-chain (listed in the trust-chain attribute, a leafref to /ne/system/security/certificates/trusted-certificate/id). Syntax: show peer-certificate[-id] [version] [serial-number] [subject-name] [issuer] [trust-chain] [valid-from] [valid-to] [status] ... [white-listed] [revocation-mode], and set peer-certificate[-id] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [revocation-mode <value>]. Settable attributes are only alarm-report-control (inhibited, allowed, default allowed), label (0..256) and revocation-mode (auto, force-revoked, force-unrevoked, default auto). status values include revoked, expired, pending-import, untrusted, future, valid and unsupported.

SSH is off by default. On the ssh command, enabled enables direct access to shell via ssh and takes true or false with a default of false, so you must set ssh enabled true to turn it on. The port attribute is the port listening for ssh login that goes directly to shell; its range is 1..65535 and the default is 8022, not 22. Syntax: set ssh [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [pre-login-message <value>] [post-login-message <value>] and show ssh [enabled] [port] [pre-login-message] [post-login-message]. pre-login-message is the welcome message displayed before user login, a string of length 0..1440 with no default; post-login-message is displayed after login, also 0..1440, and has a default warning banner stating the system is restricted to authorized users for business purposes and may be monitored. The ssh object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Add an ssh-authorized-key entry for that user. Each authorized key entry contains a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication. Syntax: add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label <value>], with set ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [label <value>], show ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [public-key-algorithm] [public-key] [label] and delete ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id>. user-name is the user owning the authorized key and can be a local or remote user, a string of length 0..32; key-id is a unique identifier (name) for the entry, a string of length 1..64. public-key is the SSHv2 (OpenSSH Portable) public key component encoded in PEM format, '<key type><SPACE>...base64 encoded OpenSSH public key...<SPACE><comment>', a string of 0..2048 characters. public-key-algorithm is show-only: ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072 or ssh-rsa4096. Example: add ssh-authorized-key-admin/1 public-key AAAAE2VjZHNhLXNoYTIt... Deleting prompts for confirmation.
